Just as other small Prussian towns, until the early 15th century, Tczew did not partake in political life of the Teutonic Order’s state. The first opportunity for Tczew townspeople to engage in independent political actions arose after the Order’s defeat in the Grunwald Battle on 15 July 1410. The Tczew citizens recognized authority of King of Poland Władysław II Jagiełło, who bestow on them the right to ferry across the Vistula in Gorzędziej. However, after the Polish army retreated from Malbork at the beginning of October 1410, Tczew townspeople took the Polish crew captive and returned under the authority of the Grand Master. In 1412, the delegates of the Tczew town council were invited by the Grand Master to the estate convention in Elbląg, during which Nicolaus, Tczew mayor, was appointed member of the State Council by Grand Master Heinrich von Plauen35. In 1440s and 1450s, the town authorities became involved in opposition activities against the Teutonic Order. In 1440, Tczew joined the Prussian Confederation which, acting as the representation of cities and knighthood, made attempts to enlist small towns for political campaigns against the Teutonic Oder. From among the small towns of Pomerelia, it was the Tczew town council who became most actively involved in the activities of the estate opposition. Between 1440 and 1453, its representatives participated in as many as six estate conventions. After the uprising of the Prussian estates against the territorial ruler broke out on 6 February 1454, the Tczew town authorities endorsed the Prussian Confederation. Due to its situation, the town played an important role in protecting navigation on the Vistula and the crossing over the river on the way to Malbork. Tczew briefly returned to the rule of the Grand Master after the Teutonic Order’s victory in the battle near Chojnice (18 September 1454). It was only after the occupation of Malbork by the armies of the Prussian Confederation and King of Poland that the mercenaries of the Teutonic Order left Tczew on 13 June 1457. A few months later, Kazimierz II Jagiełłon, King of Poland, transferred the town and the former Vogtei of Tczew to Gdańsk as collateral for the costs incurred during the conflict. The long war ended with the Second Peace of Toruń, concluded on 19 October 1466, under which Pomerelia was incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland as part of Royal Prussia36 .

In this new political, structural and territorial context, the former Vogtei of Tczew ended up within the boundary of Tczew poviat, the largest of all eight poviats in the Pomeranian county. Estimates of the population of Tczew in the Middle Ages and in the early modern era are based mainly on the data relating to the number of properties. These calculations assumed that there was an average of seven residents per house and four per buda (an urban shack without a garden attached to it). Assuming that the initial urban area was divided into approximately 56 plots, the estimated population of Tczew around 1300 amounted to approximately 400 people. A marked increase in population occurred in the late Middle Ages and the first half of the 16th century. Estimates based on data from 1570 relating to the number of houses and buildings indicate that the population of the town within the walls was around 1,100 at that time. Considering the limited development of suburban settlement, estimating the population of the entire urban complex at around 1,200 seems reasonable. Wars and epidemics which accompanied them had a negative impact on the demographic development of the town in the following two centuries. Therefore, the number of 1,201 inhabitants recorded in sources from 1772 (see Table 1) confirms the stagnation of Tczew’s population in the early modern era. As regards legal status, the population of Tczew was divided into citizens and other residents who did not have municipal rights. Citizenship in the town was granted to free persons who could present a letter of good birth as a legitimate issue of a married couple and pay the appropriate fee. The sons of Tczew citizens were exempt from this fee. Citizens had the right to purchase properties within the town and engage in trade and crafts. 37 M. Biskup, A. The ethnic structure of Tczew’s population was diverse, with residents of German origin constituting the dominant group. German was also the official language used in the town hall. Polish residents, who were fewer in number, tended to fall into the poorer social classes38 .

The economic development of Tczew in the pre-industrial era did not differ significantly from the patterns characteristic of small towns in Central and Eastern Europe, whose trade, production and service functions were focused on the surrounding region with agriculture being an indispensable part of urban life. Despite Tczew’s favourable geographical location – at the intersection of an important west-east land route and the Vistula River, which was a major trade route connecting Polish lands with the Baltic Sea – the town did not develop any lasting long-distance trade structures. Presumably the main factor limiting the development of trade in Tczew was the proximity of Gdańsk, located at the mouth of the Vistula River and having an established position in international trade. Until the beginning of the 15th century, a trade representative of the Teutonic Order resided in Tczew. He was responsible for the distribution of imported goods, in particular cloth and spices, and the purchase of products intended for export, mainly grain and timber. In medieval and early modern Tczew, there were also intermediaries representing Gdańsk merchants who purchased raw materials (primarily grain and wood supplied from the Tuchola Forest). Although insufficient sources prevent us from pinpointing the scale of Tczew’s turnover in the early modern era, it can be assumed that grain played a significant role in local trade. The annual fair in Tczew, which began every year on the Sunday after the Feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September), was regional in scope, attended by merchants and craftsmen from towns located up to 40 kilometres from Tczew. Daily commercial activity was concentrated in the market square, with permanent sales points: bread stalls, butcher’s shops, market stalls and street stalls. Weekly fairs, organised every Saturday, also played an important role. They functioned as the basic form of trade with the populations of the surrounding villages. The river harbour and the Vistula skippers, whose guild is mentioned in sources as early as 1390, were also of significant importance in the regional economy of Tczew39 . None of the crafts practised in Tczew in the pre-industrial era grew beyond local significance. In the Middle Ages, there was a fairly large group of clothiers in the town who supplied their products to i.a. Malbork Castle. However, in the early modern era, cloth production declined, with linen weavers taking over the leading role among the weaving crafts. According to the tax register from 1570, there were 106 craftsmen living in Tczew, representing 25 different manufacturing and service industries. The most numerous professions included fishermen (15 people), linen weavers (11 people), bakers (9 people), shoemakers (8 people), and blacksmiths (6 people).Other crafts included carpenters, wheelwrights and furriers (5 people each). This reveals that the structure of crafts in Tczew was diverse, but lacked specialised and clearly dominant industries. The production and sale of beer was of great importance for the economic situation of the townspeople of Tczew. However, the right to produce this beverage was granted to all owners of urban plots, but the production itself was reserved for specialised craftsmen – millers and brewers40 .

All homeowners in Tczew were also farmers, as each plot of land had fields and meadows assigned to it. The expansion of land holdings visible in the 14th century may indicate the progressive countrification of the urban economy. The importance of agriculture in the life of the town is evidenced by the fact that townspeople-farmers had their own guild from the 15th century onwards. The citizens of Tczew cultivated their fields with their own agricultural equipment, although they most often employed journeymen or tenants, who received a piece of land in return. The townspeople would sell some of their crops, mainly grain, at the local market or ship them further to Gdańsk. According to data from the 17th century, the average townsman owned one or two horses and a similar number of pigs. Sheep and cattle were also bred, but there is no accurate data on the number of these animals41 . In the pre-industrial era, Tczew was part of the Diocese of Włocławek. The parish of Tczew was probably established at the time the town was founded, as indicated by references to the first parish priest dating back to 1258 and 1260. The parish church was dedicated to the Holy Cross. The construction of a brick, three-nave church probably began at the turn of the 13th and 14th centuries and was completed in the mid-14th century. An important feature distinguishing Tczew, a small town after all, was the presence of a religious convent. In 1275, Duke Sambor II attempted to establish a Benedictine convent in Tczew, but the project did not come to fruition. However, the foundation of a Dominican monastery by Duke Mestwin II in 1289 was successful. As a result of the First Partition of Poland, Tczew was annexed to the Kingdom of Prussia. The Prussian administration entered the town on 13 September 1772, and a few days later, on 27 September, the mayor and the secretary of the council gathered in Malbork (Germ. Marienburg), where they took an oath of allegiance to King Frederick II. After the defeat of Prussia in the war with Napoleon in 1806, the town was captured as a result of a brief siege on 23 February 1807 by General Jan Henryk Dąbrowski’s division supporting the French army’s attack on Gdańsk. During the warfare, many of the town’s houses were destroyed, whereas the suburbs were completely consumed by fire. Contributions to the French army, i.a. to cover the cost of expanding the fortifications, ruined the townspeople economically. Under the terms of the Congress of Vienna of 1815, Prussia retained sovereignty over Pomerelia44 . The Constitution of 1808 defined the political system of towns in the Prussian state. Local government was placed under the control of the state authorities, which financed some of the tasks delegated to urban authorities and approved the results of municipal elections. The powers of urban authorities and citizens’ electoral rights depended on the rank of the town. Tczew was classified as a small town with a population of less than 3,500. The town council remained the most important self-government body. In addition to its legislative powers, it elected a magistrate headed by the mayor, who exercised executive power. Over the course of the 19th century, the state authorities established a number of important offices in Tczew, including a district court in 1879, a cadastral office and a merchant court. In 1887, the Tczew poviat, which had been abolished in 1818, was restored, and the town became the seat of the poviat administrator, the Landrat45 . The urban development of Tczew in the first years under the Prussian rule were significantly hindered, not only due to the destruction and economic ruin caused by the Napoleonic Wars, but also the fortifications extended by the French, and the status of a fortress granted to the town by the Prussian authorities. Until the middle of the 19th century, the medieval spatial layout in Tczew persisted without major changes. It was not until the 1830s that the demolition of the medieval walls and early modern fortifications began. However, the town still had to wait until 1868 for a permission from the Prussian authorities to dismantle the fortifications erected by French troops. In the first half of the 19th century, the town developed slowly. The hardening of the road from Berlin to Königsberg in the years 1824–1830, which ran through the town, and the erection of a pontoon bridge over the Vistula, can only be seen as a forecast of Tczew’s growing importance as a communication hub46. A breakthrough came with the expansion of the railway network. Between 1849 and 1852, a station in Tczew was built to accommodate a railway connection from Bydgoszcz to Gdańsk. In 1857, a bridge over the Vistula was put into service, over which the railway line to Malbork and on to Königsberg was routed. In 1873, Tczew gained a railway connection with Piła (Germ. Schneidemühle). Between 1888 and 1890, a new railway bridge was put into use, releasing the old bridge for road transportation. A consequence of the growing importance of Tczew’s central functions was the creation of Tczew County in 1887. The 1890s marked the beginning of a period of very intensive development of the municipal infrastructure (electrification, gas supply and sewerage systems), housing and industrial investment, which lasted until the First World War. These projects, which had the support of the Prussian state authorities, favoured inhabitants of German nationality, since obtaining the right to build a house was linked to a declaration of the ability to speak German. Similar housing estates began to be erected on the western section of Gdańska Street (railway workers’ housing cooperative on Chłodna Street) and on the site of the former Prątnica grange52 .

The population of Tczew grew steadily from 1772 to 1914. Demographic growth was characteristic of all towns in the 19th century, but the tenfold increase in the number of inhabitants of Tczew should be considered an exceptional phenomenon (see Table 2). However, throughout this period, the number of inhabitants grew at a varying rate. In the first half of the 19th century, the town’s population increased by nearly 4,000 people. However, over the next sixty years, it grew by another 12,000. In the modern era, Tczew retained its character as an ethnically and religiously diverse town. Since the end of the 19th century, there has been a noticeable increase in the German population. In an 1890 survey regarding native language, 85% of residents indicated German, 12.7% chose Polish, and 2.3% considered themselves bilingual. In 1910, the results of a similar survey were as follows: 91.7%, 6.7% and 1.55%, respectively. The religious structure did not correspond to the ethnic structure, as while the vast majority of Poles were Catholic, a significant proportion of Germans also declared this religion. At the beginning of the 20th century, there was a clear predominance of Catholics (54.17%) over Protestants (44.27%). After 1772, a Jewish population began to settle in Tczew. Its numbers grew steadily until the 1880s (515 people). In the following decades, the number of followers of Judaism declined to 195 people in 1910. In 1835, a synagogue was built on Podgórna Street. The Jewish cemetery was located outside the town limits, on a plot of land by the road to Bałdowo53 . The economic standing of Tczew in the first half of the 19th century did not differ significantly from that in the previous period. Small-scale trade, crafts and agriculture continued to form the basis of the town’s economy. The industrial era dawned in Tczew, as in other towns in the region, only in the middle of the 19th century. It was the development of railway infrastructure that accelerated industrialisation and determined the specific nature of Tczew’s economy. The potential of water transport remained underexploited. The intensive development of agriculture in the vicinity of Tczew ensured that agricultural machinery and metal product factories, as well as food industry factories, were among the first industrial plants to be established. The expansion of the railway infrastructure (mentioned above) was also an important stimulus for the development of the machine industry. The modernisation of municipal infrastructure was a characteristic feature of the development of most towns in Pomerania and Prussia at the turn of the 19th and 20th centuries. This process also affected Tczew, whose authorities made several investments starting from the 1890s that significantly increased the town’s economic potential and improved the quality of life of its residents. A modern municipal slaughterhouse was opened in the Nowe Miasto district in 1893, while in 1898–1899 a municipal power plant was commissioned. This enabled the use of electric power in public spaces. The next stage in the development of infrastructure was the launch of the municipal water supply system in 1904, for which a water tower over 40 metres in height was built, constituting one of the characteristic elements of the town’s panorama from the west and south. The construction of the municipal sewage system, connected to the sewage treatment plant on Sambora Street, began in 1908. The implementation of this investment, in conjunction with the existing water supply system, created the conditions for the launch of a modern municipal bathhouse in 1911, serving both hygienic and social functions. Back in the 1860s, a private company began producing gas in Tczew. The takeover of the gasworks by a municipal company in 1907 enabled the modernisation of the plant and an acceleration of its productivity54 .

At the end of the 19th century, the modernisation process also included the expansion of hospital facilities. In 1877, the municipal authorities financed the establishment of a small hospital specialising in infectious diseases. In general, however, until the outbreak of World War I, hospital care in Tczew was confessional in nature. In contrast to the intense social and urban changes that took place in Tczew in the 19th century, the sacral topography of the town did not undergo any significant transformations during this period. The only significant event that had a lasting impact on the local religious landscape was the dissolution of the Dominican monastery, which had been operating in the town for over six centuries, as a result of a decision made by the Prussian authorities in 1818. The monastery buildings were adapted for the needs of municipal education, while the monastery church, then dedicated to St. Nicholas, was handed over to the Catholic parish, which was unable to use the Holy Cross Church due to its poor technical condition. After a thorough renovation of their mother church, in 1853 the Catholics handed over the former Dominican church to the Protestant community, which gave it a new name, St. George’s. The end of the 19th century brought some changes to the religious topography due to spatial development. In 1898, a new Protestant parish was established in the Nowe Miasto (New Town) district. In 1915, the Catholic Church also began efforts to establish a separate parish in this district, and a year later a committee was formed to build the St. Joseph’s Church56 .

The establishment of Catholic and Protestant parish schools in former monastery buildings initiated the process of the transformation of religious schools into municipal public schools, which was completed in 1838. In the second half of the 19th century, the municipal authorities took steps to expand the elementary school system and establish higher education institutions for boys and girls. In 1891, the public school was divided into a girls’ school, which continued to operate in the former monastery buildings, and a boys’ school, which was located in a neighbouring building on what is now St. Gregory’s Square. In the same year, an elementary school was also built in Nowe Miasto. An elementary school had also been functioning in the village of Czyżykowo since at least 1838; in 1906, a year before the village was incorporated into Tczew, it was transformed into a public primary school. In 1894, a small one-class elementary school building was built in the Tczew Meadows area . Secondary education for boys and girls developed according to a similar pattern. A secondary school for boys was established in 1876, and four years later it was given a new building on what is now Obrońców Westerplatte Street. The defeat of the German Reich in World War I and the provisions of the Treaty of Versailles resulted in the return of Pomerelia to the Polish state. Early on, the Polish administrative authority in Tczew was represented by the people’s council established in December 1918. The entry of General Józef Haller’s army into the town on 30 January 1920 marked the formal incorporation of the town into the reborn Republic of Poland. Under the new political conditions, Tczew retained its status as a county town. After 1920, a significant number of German residents left the town, and were replaced by Poles coming from the Free City of Gdańsk and Pomerelia. The immigration of Polish people to Tczew allowed for a continuation of the positive demographic trend that had been ongoing since the 19th century. From 1921 to 1939, the number of inhabitants increased by two thirds, from 16,251 to 25,530 people. The share of the German population fell from 92% in the period before the outbreak of World War I to 28% percent in 1921 and 9% in 1931.

Migration also caused changes in the religious structure, which mainly consisted of the growing predominance of Catholics. In 1936, they constituted nearly 93% of the population. The interwar period saw a marked increase in Jewish exodus, which had already become apparent in the last decades of the 19th century. In 1931, there were 103 Jews living in Tczew, and in 1939, only 18. The ethnic structure of the town changed dramatically during World War II. In the autumn of 1939 and the first months of the following year, the German occupiers murdered the most socially and politically active Poles. The last Jews living in Tczew were also murdered and the synagogue was demolished. During the war, about 1,800 Polish families were displaced, and over 3,000 Germans from the Baltic states and Bessarabia settled in their place58 . In the early years of the reborn Polish state, Tczew’s economy faced difficulties resulting from the severance of previous contacts with former markets and sources of raw materials for industry. As before, industry remained crucial to the town’s development. The structure of industrial production did not change significantly – the machinery, food, wood and building materials industries continued to dominate. However, the exodus of the German population caused significant changes in the ownership structure: most industrial plants passed into Polish hands. The development of residential as well as public housing in Tczew during the interwar period consisted mainly of the densification of districts designed before the First World War. The result of this work was a significant increase in the number of residential buildings, from 931 in 1910 to 1,586 in 1938. The construction of houses on today’s Paderewskiego Street began in 1920s as part of the development of vacant space in areas laid out in the second half of the 19th century. In the 1930s construction work resumed on Osiedle za Parkiem, where plots of land on Wybickiego and Wyspiańskiego Streets, which had already been planned, were developed. In 1935, a modern building for a public school for the German minority was opened on Parkowa Street. The town’s southern routes, including Bałdowska Street and 30 Stycznia Street, saw a wave of new villa-style houses being built. The development of the New Town area gained momentum from the late 1920s, with multi-family buildings primarily constructed on Gdańska, Kaszubska, and Pomorska Streets. An important element in the development of this district was the erection of the St. Joseph Parish Church (1936) and the establishment of a new cemetery on Gdańska Street (1930). On the northwestern outskirts of the town, the settlement of Prątnica continued to be developed. The erection of military barracks (1928–1939) on today’s Wojska Polskiego Street can be considered a forerunner of the urbanization of the western edges of the town. From 1934 onward, a spontaneous settlement of the poor began to take form in the northern part of the town, in the vicinity of workers’ allotment gardens. The first cohesive development plans in the history of Tczew were drawn up for the southern and northern districts in 1938 and 1939, but their implementation was stopped by the outbreak of World War II. No new urban development projects were undertaken during the German occupation. The land in the New Town and in Czyżków, where multi-family houses were erected on Wiejska and Nowowiejska Streets, was used for residential development. As a result of the Soviet aviation bombardments and ongoing warfare, about 14% of residential buildings were permanently damaged or destroyed. However, compared to other towns in the region, Tczew’s spoils of war were moderate. In the first postwar years, the primary investments focused on the reconstruction and modernization of the communications network and municipal infrastructure. The largest project of that time was the construction of a new railroad station in 195062. Due to the lack of financial resources, the municipal authorities adopted a development program limited to the pre-war spatial layout. For this reason, the 1952 incorporation of the territory of the former village of Suchostrzygi, located on the western side of national road no. 1 (now no. 91), did not radically change the urban character of the town. At the end of the 1950s, the area between Sobieskiego and Warsztatowa Streets was allocated for the construction of blocks of flats. In the early 1960s, the first blocks of flats were built in the Prątnica Housing Estate, but single-family houses played a crucial role in its expansion. An extensive housing estate on the southern edge of Czyżykowo (now Konarskiego Housing Estate) was being constructed simultaneously. Another such a large investment was the Śródmieście II Housing Estate (now the Garnuszewski Estate) in the western part of the town between Gdańska and Wojska Polskiego streets. These two large housing estates were part of a comprehensive urban planning concept developed in the early 1970s, according to which the Old Town was to serve as an administrative and service and commercial centre, while new residential districts were to develop in the southern and western districts. An extensive housing development in Suchostrzygi, began in the 1970s, was a part of the implementation of this concept. In the 1990s, former Piątkowo and Malinowo granges were allocated for residential purposes63. Currently, the town’s area is 22.38 square kilometers (2013 data).
